optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Straightforward type extension. BF16 support is already partially implemented.

kernels.estimated_current_efficiency: 55-65% — Dequantize kernels are memory-bound and reasonably well-implemented for most quant types. The main gap is the missing optimized Q8_0→FP16 kernel (CUDA has a 2-3x faster variant). Missing sub-group size attributes hurt occupancy. NC support gap forces extra copies for non-contiguous quantized tensors. The reorder variants (q4_0, q4_K, q6_K) are SYCL-specific optimizations that are ahead of CUDA.

kernels.name: binbcast (binary broadcast) SYCL kernels

launch_config.global_size_expression: 3D adaptive: block_dims = (min(ne2*ne3, cap), min(ne1, cap), min(hne0, 128)) where cap fills to 128; fallback 1D: ceil_div(ne0*ne1*ne2*ne3, 128) when z-dim exceeds 65535
launch_config.notes: Two kernel variants: k_bin_bcast (3D grid) and k_bin_bcast_unravel (1D fallback). Block size is 128 matching CUDA. The 3D grid packs dimensions 2 and 3 into the z-axis using integer division (ne2*ne3 packed). The dimension 0 uses hne0 = max(ne0/2, 1) which halves the grid in dimension 0. Missing [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size]] on both kernel launch paths. Fallback condition only checks z-dim > 65535, while CUDA checks both y AND z — potential bug for large ne1.

strided_accesses: src1 broadcast: i10 = i0 % ne10 causes non-contiguous access when ne10 < ne0
src0/src1 stride-based addressing via s01/s02/s03 and s11/s12/s13
memory_patterns.notes: Innermost loop iterates over dimension 0 with stride equal to total threads in dimension 0. Consecutive threads access consecutive elements in src0 and dst (coalesced). src1 access is coalesced only when ne10 >= ne0 (no broadcast in dim 0); otherwise the modulo causes irregular access. All loads/stores are scalar — no sycl::vec usage.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. Pure element-wise operations with no inter-thread data sharing.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reductions — each thread computes one or more output elements independently.

data_types.notes: All binary ops compute in float regardless of input/output types. Supports 6 type combinations: f32/f32/f32, f16/f16/f16, f16/f32/f16, i32/i32/i32, i16/i16/i16. SYCL has i32 and i16 support that CUDA lacks. CUDA additionally supports f16/f32/f32 which SYCL does not.

math_functions.notes: No transcendental math — only add, sub, mul, div operations. div uses standard float division. No optimization opportunities for native math.

hot_loops: k_bin_bcast inner loop (line 44-48): iterates ne0/(block_dims[2]*block_nums[2]) times — handles multiple elements per thread in dimension 0
Dimension collapse loop (lines 127-139): host-side, iterates up to 3 times to collapse non-broadcast dimensions
loop_analysis.notes: The inner loop in k_bin_bcast cannot be unrolled since ne0 is runtime. The loop body is simple (one load from each src + one op + one store). k_bin_bcast_unravel has no loop — one element per thread.

anti_patterns: Uses plain integer % and / for broadcast index computation (i1%ne11, i2%ne12, i3%ne13, i0%ne10, i/(ne2*ne1*ne0) in unravel) — CUDA uses fastdiv/fastmodulo with multiply-high (2-3 cycles vs 20-30 cycles for integer division on GPU)
DPCT artifact: dpct::has_capability_or_fail(fp16) called on every launch
DPCT artifact: stale DPCT1049 comment at lines 240-245
Missing [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size]] on both launch paths
Fallback condition only checks block_nums[0] > 65535 — CUDA checks both y AND z grid limits; missing y check is a potential correctness bug for large ne1
Missing fused multi-source op support — CUDA's variadic template fuses up to 8 add operations into a single kernel launch, eliminating redundant memory traffic
Missing repeat_back kernel — CUDA has k_repeat_back for the inverse of repeat
s00 is GGML_UNUSED instead of GGML_ASSERT(s00 == 1) — CUDA asserts this for safety

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace plain integer % and / with fast division/modulo for broadcast index computation. CUDA uses fastdiv/fastmodulo which precomputes magic numbers and uses multiply-high + shift (2-3 cycles) instead of hardware integer division (20-30 cycles on GPU). In binbcast, every thread executes 3-4 modulo operations (i1%ne11, i2%ne12, i3%ne13, i0%ne10) and the unravel kernel adds 3-4 integer divisions (i/(ne2*ne1*ne0) etc.). This is the single largest performance gap vs CUDA for this kernel.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 15-40% speedup depending on tensor dimensions. For small-element broadcast ops (where compute per element is minimal: add/sub = 1 FLOP), the division overhead dominates. The unravel kernel (1D fallback) is worst affected — 7+ divisions per thread vs 0 with fastdiv.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Implement a SYCL fastdiv utility matching CUDA's: precompute (mp, L, divisor) triple on host for each ne value, pass as kernel parameters. Replace % with fastmodulo and / with fastdiv in both k_bin_bcast and k_bin_bcast_unravel. The host-side init_fastdiv_values() computes: L = ceil(log2(d)), mp = 2^(32+L)/d + 1. The device-side fastdiv uses __umulhi(n, mp) >> L. On SYCL/Intel, use sycl::mul_hi for the multiply-high operation.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The fastdiv algorithm requires careful handling of edge cases (divisor = 1, power of 2 divisors). CUDA's implementation is proven correct. Need to verify sycl::mul_hi behavior matches __umulhi for unsigned 32-bit multiply-high.

optimization_opportunities.description: Implement fused multi-source binary broadcast operations matching CUDA's ggml_cuda_op_fused_add. CUDA uses variadic templates (src1_ptrs...) with C++17 fold expressions to fuse up to 8 add operations into a single kernel launch. This eliminates N-1 kernel launches and N-1 redundant reads/writes of the destination tensor for N fused operations. In transformer inference, multiple bias additions or residual connections can be fused.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 30-50% throughput improvement for fusible add chains. For a chain of N adds, reduces memory traffic from 3N passes (read src0 + read src1 + write dst per add) to N+2 passes (read src0 + N src1 reads + 1 write). Also eliminates N-1 kernel launch overheads.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add variadic template parameter pack src1_ptrs to k_bin_bcast and bin_bcast_sycl. Use C++17 fold expression: result = (..., (result = bin_op(result, (float)src1s[i_src1 + i10]))). Add ggml_sycl_op_fused_add dispatch function that detects fusible add chains in the op graph and batches them. Requires modifications to ggml-sycl.cpp dispatch logic to detect fusible patterns.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires op graph analysis to detect fusible patterns. The variadic template approach requires careful handling of different tensor shapes and broadcast patterns across fused operations. Need to ensure all fused sources have compatible broadcast dimensions.

optimization_opportunities.description: Fix the fallback condition to check both y and z grid dimension limits, matching CUDA. Currently SYCL only checks block_nums[0] > 65535 (z-dimension equivalent) but not block_nums[1] (y-dimension). CUDA checks both: block_nums.z > 65535 || block_nums.y > 65535. If ne1 is very large (>65535 * block_dims[1]), the SYCL kernel could fail or produce incorrect results.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Correctness fix — prevents potential failures with large ne1 dimensions.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change the condition at line 221 from: if (block_nums[0] > 65535) to: if (block_nums[0] > 65535 || block_nums[1] > 65535). This ensures the 1D fallback kernel is used whenever any grid dimension exceeds SYCL limits.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Simple conditional change. The unravel fallback kernel already handles arbitrary dimensions correctly.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to both kernel launch paths (k_bin_bcast and k_bin_bcast_unravel). Without this attribute, the compiler may choose SIMD32 on Xe2, halving occupancy for these memory-bound kernels.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-10% from better occupancy and latency hiding.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add the attribute to both parallel_for lambdas at lines 232 and 251.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No sub-group operations are used. Only affects SIMD width selection.

optimization_opportunities.description: Implement repeat_back kernel. CUDA has k_repeat_back for the inverse of repeat (summing elements that were repeated back to the original size using atomicAdd). SYCL binbcast does not have this, which may cause fallback to CPU or incorrect behavior for backward pass of repeat operations.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Feature completeness — enables SYCL backward pass for repeat operations without CPU fallback.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Port CUDA's k_repeat_back kernel: for each output element, use atomicAdd to accumulate contributions from all repeated input elements. Use sycl::atomic_ref<float, ...> for the atomic operation. The kernel iterates over repeat dimensions and accumulates.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Atomic operations on float require sycl::atomic_ref with memory_order::relaxed. Need to verify Intel GPU support for float atomics. The atomic approach may have contention for small output tensors.

optimization_opportunities.description: Clean up DPCT artifacts: remove dpct::has_capability_or_fail(fp16) check, delete stale DPCT1049 comment, replace __dpct_inline__ on op functions in binbcast.hpp. Also add GGML_ASSERT(s00 == 1) to match CUDA's safety check instead of GGML_UNUSED(s00).
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Minor: removes per-dispatch capability query overhead. Code quality improvement.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Remove dpct::has_capability_or_fail blocks (lines 225-226, 246-247). Delete DPCT comment (lines 240-245). Replace __dpct_inline__ with inline in binbcast.hpp. Change GGML_UNUSED(s00) to GGML_ASSERT(s00 == 1).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Mechanical cleanup. The s00 assert adds a safety check that CUDA already has.

kernels.estimated_current_efficiency: 50-60% — Binary broadcast kernels are memory-bound but waste significant cycles on expensive integer division for broadcast index computation (CUDA uses fastdiv for 10x cheaper division). Missing fused multi-source support leaves significant throughput on the table for common add chains. The dimension collapse optimization and 3D grid mapping are well-implemented, matching CUDA. Missing repeat_back is a feature gap.

kernels.name: cpy SYCL kernels

launch_config.work_group_size: 32 for scalar copy kernels (SYCL_CPY_BLOCK_SIZE); 1 for quantized f32->q and q->f32 kernels; 32 for q->q same-type copy kernels
launch_config.global_size_expression: ceil_div(ne, SYCL_CPY_BLOCK_SIZE) for scalar; ne/qk for f32->q; ne for q->f32; ceil_div(ne, SYCL_CPY_BLOCK_SIZE) for q->q
launch_config.notes: CRITICAL: Quantized f32->q and q->f32 kernels launch with work-group size 1 — each quantization block processed by single work-item. Catastrophically bad on Xe2 where 15/16 SIMD lanes are idle. CUDA also uses block size 1 for these but NVIDIA warp scheduling partially compensates. Scalar copy work-group of 32 is also too small (CUDA uses 64). All kernels use 3D nd_range with first 2 dims = 1 (DPCT artifact). No [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size]] on any kernel.

strided_accesses: Non-contiguous tensor paths: byte offsets nb00-nb03 and nb10-nb13 can produce strided access per element
Quantized single-thread kernels: 32 sequential scalar loads by one thread — no sub-group cooperation for coalescing
memory_patterns.notes: All loads/stores are scalar — one element per work-item. sycl::vec<float,1> used at line 22 only for f32->f16 conversion, not for vectorized memory access. Contiguous tensor copies (the common case) have coalesced access in scalar kernels (adjacent threads access adjacent elements). Quantized kernels have no coalescing — single thread reads 32 floats sequentially. Missing contiguous fast-path: dispatch always uses full 4D index decomposition (12 integer divisions/multiplies per element) even when both tensors are contiguous.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM usage in any cpy kernel. CUDA version has 32x33 float shared memory tile for transposed copy (cpy_scalar_transpose, cpy.cu line 59) — this optimization is entirely missing in the SYCL version.

reduction_pattern.notes: Quantization helpers (cpy.hpp) contain serial reductions within single work-items: amax/vmax loops of 32 elements (cpy_blck_f32_q8_0 line 34, cpy_blck_f32_q4_0 line 58, cpy_blck_f32_q5_0 line 122, cpy_blck_f32_q5_1 line 157, cpy_blck_f32_iq4_nl line 191). These could use sub-group reduction if the work-group size were > 1 with cooperative processing.

data_types.notes: FP32 compute throughout. For copy operations this is appropriate since the operation is just type conversion. Quantization math (amax, scaling) benefits from FP32 precision.

math_functions.notes: Standard precision math throughout. The 1.0f/d reciprocal (computed once per quantization block) could use sycl::native::recip for marginal speedup, but the impact is minimal since it's computed only once per 32 elements. sycl::round is acceptable as-is.

hot_loops: cpy_blck_f32_q8_0: amax loop (cpy.hpp:34, 32 iters) + quantize loop (cpy.hpp:44, 32 iters)
cpy_blck_f32_q4_0: amax loop (cpy.hpp:58, 32 iters) + pack loop (cpy.hpp:71, 16 iters)
cpy_blck_f32_q4_1: min/max loop (cpy.hpp:90, 32 iters) + pack loop (cpy.hpp:103, 16 iters)
cpy_blck_f32_q5_0: amax loop (cpy.hpp:122, 32 iters) + pack loop (cpy.hpp:136, 16 iters)
cpy_blck_f32_q5_1: min/max loop (cpy.hpp:157, 31 iters) + pack loop (cpy.hpp:170, 16 iters)
cpy_blck_f32_iq4_nl: amax loop (cpy.hpp:191, 32 iters) + index search + accumulate loop (cpy.hpp:203, 16 iters)
cpy_blck_q8_0_f32: dequant loop (cpy.cpp:94, 16 iters)
cpy_blck_q_f32: dequant loop (cpy.cpp:107, qk/2 iters)
loop_analysis.notes: No #pragma unroll on any loop in cpy.hpp or cpy.cpp. CUDA's cpy.cu has #pragma unroll on dequant loops (lines 97, 110). All loop trip counts are compile-time constants (QK8_0=32, QK4_0=32, etc.) making them ideal candidates for unrolling.

anti_patterns: CRITICAL: Work-group size of 1 for all quantized copy kernels (cpy.cpp lines 256,268,281,293,307,319,333,345,359,371,385) — 16x SIMD underutilization
Work-group size of 32 (SYCL_CPY_BLOCK_SIZE, presets.hpp:35) for scalar copies — should be 256+ for Xe2
3D nd_range<3> for logically 1D work on ALL kernel launches (DPCT artifact)
Manual thread indexing (item_ct1.get_local_range(2)*item_ct1.get_group(2)+item_ct1.get_local_id(2)) instead of get_global_id() (lines 58, 121, 148, 175)
dpct::has_capability_or_fail() on every launch (lines 202, 220, 238, 398) — unnecessary runtime overhead
__dpct_inline__ instead of standard inline (cpy.hpp:9)
dpct::min() instead of std::min() (cpy.hpp:75,107,140)
item_ct1 naming convention (DPCT artifact) throughout
Missing contiguous fast-path for mixed-type copies: always performs 12 integer div/mul for 4D index decomposition even when tensors are contiguous (cpy.cpp lines 66-76)
Missing transposed copy kernel with SLM tiling (CUDA has cpy_scalar_transpose with shared memory)
int32 indices instead of int64 — potential overflow for large tensors (lines 54-76)
No #pragma unroll on any quantization loop (cpy.hpp) or dequantization loop (cpy.cpp:94,107)
No [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] on any kernel
Missing BF16 copy support (CUDA has f32->bf16, bf16->f32, bf16->f16, etc.)

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase quantized copy kernel work-group size from 1 to at least 16 (one sub-group). Currently each f32->q and q->f32 kernel launches with work-group size 1 (cpy.cpp lines 256, 268, 281, 293, 307, 319, 333, 345, 359, 371, 385). On Xe2, this wastes 15/16 of each SIMD lane since the native SIMD width is 16. Even without restructuring the algorithm, launching with work-group size 16 allows the hardware to pack 16 independent quantization blocks into one SIMD thread, achieving full lane utilization. The kernel code already uses per-thread indexing (each thread processes one block independently), so increasing the work-group size from 1 to 16/32/64 is a trivial dispatch change.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 4-8x throughput improvement for quantized copy operations. Currently 15/16 SIMD lanes are wasted. Proper work-group sizing fills all lanes and enables better latency hiding through concurrent work-groups.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change from sycl::nd_range<3>((1,1,num_blocks), (1,1,1)) to sycl::nd_range<1>(ceil_div(num_blocks,256)*256, 256) for all f32->q and q->f32 dispatches. Each work-item still processes one quantization block independently — no algorithm change needed. The kernel already has an early-return guard (i >= ne). For q->f32 kernels, note that num_blocks = ne (number of elements), not ne/qk, so the grid may need adjustment.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No algorithm change — only dispatch configuration. Each work-item is fully independent. The early-return guard (if i >= ne) already handles excess threads.

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase SYCL_CPY_BLOCK_SIZE from 32 to 256. The scalar copy kernels (f32->f32, f32->f16, f16->f32, f16->f16, i16->i16, i32->i32) use a work-group size of 32 (presets.hpp line 35). On Xe2, this is only 2 sub-groups of 16, severely limiting occupancy and latency hiding. CUDA uses 64 which is already small. The Intel GPU Optimization Guide recommends 256 or 512 for best performance. Since each work-item processes one element independently, increasing to 256 is a trivial change with no algorithm impact.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 30-50% throughput improvement for scalar copy operations. Larger work-groups improve memory latency hiding through more concurrent threads per Xe-core. The current 32-thread work-group uses only 1/4 of the occupancy potential of a 128-thread work-group.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change SYCL_CPY_BLOCK_SIZE from 32 to 256 in presets.hpp line 35. Also change the q_q same-type copy kernels (lines 452-510) which also use SYCL_CPY_BLOCK_SIZE. Verify no other kernels depend on this constant. Alternatively, define a separate CPY_BLOCK_SIZE_SCALAR constant to avoid affecting other users of SYCL_CPY_BLOCK_SIZE.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No algorithm change. Check if SYCL_CPY_BLOCK_SIZE is used by other kernels — if so, create a separate constant for copy kernels.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add contiguous fast-path for mixed-type scalar copies. Currently, all scalar copy kernels (f32->f32, f32->f16, f16->f32, etc.) unconditionally perform 4D index decomposition with 12 integer divisions/multiplies per element (cpy.cpp lines 66-76). For contiguous tensors — the most common case — this index math is entirely redundant since element i maps directly to byte offset i*sizeof(element). CUDA has a separate cpy_scalar_contiguous kernel (cpy.cu line 172) for this case. The dispatch at line 525 only uses memcpy for same-type contiguous copies, falling through to the expensive strided path for mixed-type contiguous copies like f32->f16.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 40-60% throughput improvement for contiguous mixed-type copies (e.g., f32->f16 contiguous). The 4D index decomposition dominates execution time for this memory-bound operation — each element requires 12 integer divisions that could be replaced with a single address offset. This is the most impactful optimization for copy kernels.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Add a contiguous fast-path kernel like CUDA's cpy_scalar_contiguous: template<cpy_kernel_t cpy_1> static void cpy_contiguous(const char * cx, char * cdst, const int ne, const int nb_src, const int nb_dst, nd_item<1> item). 2. In each dispatch function, detect contiguous case (ggml_is_contiguous()) and call the fast-path. 3. Alternatively, modify ggml_sycl_cpy at line 525 to detect contiguous + different types and dispatch to the fast kernel. The fast kernel: int i = item.get_global_id(0); if (i >= ne) return; cpy_1(cx + i*nb_src, cdst + i*nb_dst);
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: CUDA already implements this pattern (cpy_scalar_contiguous). The contiguity check is already available via ggml_is_contiguous(). The fast-path is a strict simplification of the general path.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add vectorized loads/stores (sycl::vec<float, 4>) to the contiguous scalar copy kernels. Currently each work-item reads and writes exactly 1 element. For f32->f32 copy, using vec4 reduces memory transactions by 4x. For f32->f16, each work-item can load vec4<float> and store vec4<half> in a single transaction. Copy kernels are purely memory-bound (0 compute ops per byte), so maximizing memory throughput is critical.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 20-40% throughput improvement for contiguous copy operations. Combined with the contiguous fast-path (opt_007_003), this can achieve near-peak memory bandwidth for simple copies.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: For the contiguous fast-path (requires opt_007_003 first), create a vec4 variant: each work-item processes 4 elements using sycl::vec<T,4> loads and stores. For f32->f16, load vec4<float>, convert to vec4<half> using vec.convert<>(), store vec4<half>. Grid size reduces by 4x. Handle tail elements (ne % 4 != 0) with scalar fallback. For non-contiguous paths, vectorization is not applicable due to non-uniform byte offsets. Ref: optimization_guide.md section 2.2.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires contiguous fast-path (opt_007_003) as a prerequisite. Vectorization only applies to contiguous case where alignment is guaranteed. Tail handling is straightforward.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add #pragma unroll to all quantization and dequantization inner loops. All loops in cpy.hpp (amax, quantize, pack) and cpy.cpp (dequant) have compile-time constant trip counts (QK8_0=32, QK4_0=32, etc.) but lack unroll pragmas. CUDA's cpy.cu has #pragma unroll on dequant loops (lines 97, 110). On Intel GPUs, #pragma unroll reduces loop overhead and enables register allocation across iterations, improving IPC for these short tight loops.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-20% speedup for quantized copy operations. The effect is more pronounced when combined with work-group size increase (opt_007_001) since more threads means higher total throughput where the per-thread loop efficiency matters.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add #pragma unroll before each loop in cpy.hpp: line 34 (amax q8_0), line 44 (quantize q8_0), line 58 (amax q4_0), line 71 (pack q4_0), line 90 (min/max q4_1), line 103 (pack q4_1), line 122 (amax q5_0), line 136 (pack q5_0), line 157 (min/max q5_1), line 170 (pack q5_1), line 191 (amax iq4_nl), line 203 (search+pack iq4_nl). In cpy.cpp: line 94 (dequant q8_0), line 107 (dequant generic). Total: 14 pragma insertions.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: All loop trip counts are compile-time constants. #pragma unroll is a compiler hint that cannot cause incorrect behavior. At worst, the compiler ignores it.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to all kernel launches. No cpy kernel specifies the required sub-group size. On Xe2, the compiler should be directed to use SIMD16 (the native width) to ensure optimal lane utilization and prevent the compiler from choosing SIMD32 which would halve occupancy. This is especially important when combined with work-group size increases (opt_007_001, opt_007_002).
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% improvement from guaranteed optimal SIMD width selection. Without this attribute, the compiler may choose SIMD32 which reduces hardware thread count by 2x.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to each parallel_for lambda in cpy.cpp. There are approximately 22 kernel launches: 6 scalar type copies (lines 204-445), 11 quantized conversions (lines 256-390), 5 same-type quantized copies (lines 448-510). Ref: optimization_guide.md section 1.2.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No sub-group operations are used in copy kernels, so this only affects the compiler's SIMD width selection. No functional impact.

optimization_opportunities.description: Clean up DPCT migration artifacts: (1) Convert all nd_range<3> to nd_range<1> since work is logically 1D. (2) Replace manual thread indexing with get_global_id(0). (3) Remove dpct::has_capability_or_fail() calls (lines 202, 220, 238, 398). (4) Replace dpct::min() with std::min() in cpy.hpp (lines 75, 107, 140). (5) Replace __dpct_inline__ with standard inline (cpy.hpp line 9). (6) Rename item_ct1 to item throughout.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Minor: removes per-launch device capability queries (~microseconds). get_global_id() may enable minor compiler optimizations vs manual index arithmetic. Primary benefit is code clarity and maintainability.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Mechanical refactoring across ~22 kernel launches in cpy.cpp and helper functions in cpy.hpp. The dpct::has_capability_or_fail removal is the most impactful — it's called 4 times per f16-related kernel launch and does a synchronous device query.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Purely mechanical refactoring with no algorithmic changes.

optimization_opportunities.description: Upgrade int32 indices to int64 for large tensor support. All index computations (lines 54-76, 117-141, 144-168, 170-194) use int32 which overflows for tensors with more than ~2 billion elements. CUDA's cpy.cu uses int64_t throughout. Modern LLMs with long context windows can have tensors exceeding this limit.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Correctness fix for large tensors. No performance impact for typical sizes. May have minor performance impact on Xe2 due to wider integer operations, but correctness is paramount.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change all int parameters (ne, ne00, ne01, ne02, nb00-nb13, etc.) to int64_t in cpy_f32_f16, cpy_f32_q, cpy_q_f32, cpy_q_q kernel templates and all dispatch functions. Also update the product computations (ne00*ne01*ne02) which are the first to overflow. This is a mechanical change affecting function signatures throughout cpy.cpp.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: int64 arithmetic is slightly slower than int32 on GPUs. The main risk is ensuring all callers pass int64 consistently and that the SYCL backend tensor metadata is properly cast.

kernels.estimated_current_efficiency: 20-30% — Copy kernels are severely underperforming due to catastrophically small work-group sizes (1 for quantized, 32 for scalar), missing contiguous fast-path (needless 12 integer div/mul per element), no vectorized loads, and numerous DPCT migration artifacts. The quantized copy path in particular is ~16x slower than necessary due to single-work-item SIMD underutilization.

kernels.name: mmq SYCL kernels

launch_config.work_group_size: nwarps * WARP_SIZE (varies by compute capability: AMPERE path uses 4*32=128 for XMX, 4*32=128 for non-XMX; RDNA2 uses 8*32=256; RDNA1 uses 8*32=256; PASCAL uses 8*32=256). The XMX path tile sizes are tiny: mmq_x=4, mmq_y=32 — designed for small batch sizes with tensor cores, but no actual XMX/tensor core compute is used.
launch_config.global_size_expression: nd_range<3>((1, block_num_y, block_num_x) * (1, nwarps, WARP_SIZE)) where block_num_x = ceil(nrows_x/mmq_y), block_num_y = ceil(ncols_y/mmq_x)
launch_config.notes: The dispatch selects tile sizes based on compute_capability (VER_GEN13/GEN12/GEN9/4VEC) but the kernel itself is hardcoded to use AMPERE constants — the per-quant-type kernel functions like mul_mat_q4_0 always use MMQ_X_Q4_0_AMPERE, MMQ_Y_Q4_0_AMPERE, NWARPS_Q4_0_AMPERE regardless of runtime selection. This means the host dispatches with one tile size but the kernel uses a different one — a serious bug if the cc >= VER_GEN12 or >= VER_GEN13 paths are taken. The 3D nd_range has first dim always 1 (DPCT artifact). No [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size]] on any kernel.

strided_accesses: X tile loading: each warp loads mmq_y/nwarps rows × WARP_SIZE columns — coalesced across the K dimension
Y tile loading: non-optimal — reads block_q8_1 structs from global memory per iteration instead of using a reformatted layout like CUDA's block_q8_1_mmq
memory_patterns.notes: All loads are 32-bit scalar (get_int_from_uint8, get_int_from_int8). CUDA's MMA path uses __ldmatrix for 128-bit vectorized shared→register loads. The Y loading pattern reads from global memory on every K sub-iteration (qr times), while CUDA pre-formats Y data into block_q8_1_mmq tiles for conflict-free shared memory access.

slm_usage.slm_bytes: Varies by quant type and tile size. For Q4_0 non-XMX (mmq_x=64, mmq_y=128): tile_x_qs = 128*(32+1)*4 = 16896B, tile_x_d = 128*(32/8+128/8)*4 = varies, tile_y_qs = 64*32*4 = 8192B, tile_y_ds = 64*32/8*4 = 1024B. Total ~26-30KB per work-group. For XMX (mmq_x=4, mmq_y=32): much smaller ~2-3KB.
slm_usage.notes: SLM tiling uses +1 padding per row (stride = WARP_SIZE+1 or 2*WARP_SIZE+1) for bank conflict avoidance on 32-bit accesses — matches CUDA's dp4a path. However, this padding was designed for NVIDIA's 32-bank scheme; Intel Xe2 has different SLM banking (16 banks of 4 bytes each) so the padding may not be optimal. No double-buffering of Y tiles. Global barrier (item_ct1.barrier()) used between load and compute phases — should use barrier(access::fence_space::local_space) since only SLM is accessed.

reduction_pattern.notes: No explicit reduction — the output is a direct accumulation per (row, col) element with each thread computing its own partial sum across the K dimension. The K-dimension is iterated in the outer loop (ib0 loop) with barrier synchronization between tiles.

data_types.compute_type: float (accumulation in FP32, quantized weights as int via dp4a)
data_types.notes: The CUDA version has a full MMA (tensor core) path using int8 tensor core operations (mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k32.row.col.s32.s8.s8.s32) for Turing+ and AMD MFMA for CDNA. Intel Xe2's XMX (Matrix Extension) supports int8 via SYCL joint_matrix, but the SYCL version has NO XMX path despite #define SYCL_USE_XMX existing — the define only changes tile sizes, not the compute method. This is the single largest performance gap.

functions: dpct::dp4a (used in all vec_dot_*_impl functions for int8 dot product)
dpct::vectorized_binary<sycl::char4> with dpct::sub_sat() (q5_0, q3_K, q6_K dequant)
dpct::min (bounds checking in load_tiles and mul_mat_q)
math_functions.notes: dpct::dp4a maps to Intel's dp4a instruction which is efficient on Xe2. However, dpct::vectorized_binary<sycl::char4>(a, b, dpct::sub_sat()) is a DPCT compatibility function that may not compile to optimal byte-level SIMD — should use Intel-native byte operations or sycl::vec<int8_t,4> arithmetic.

hot_loops: mul_mat_q outer K loop: for (ib0 = 0; ib0 < blocks_per_row_x; ib0 += blocks_per_warp) — iterates blocks_per_row_x/blocks_per_warp times (line 1228)
mul_mat_q inner qr loop: for (ir = 0; ir < qr; ++ir) — iterates qr times (2-8 depending on quant type) (line 1236)
mul_mat_q innermost K loop: for (k = ir*WARP_SIZE/qr; k < (ir+1)*WARP_SIZE/qr; k += vdr) — compute-bound inner loop (line 1290)
vec_dot output accumulation: 2 nested loops over mmq_y/WARP_SIZE × mmq_x/nwarps (lines 1292-1300)
load_tiles per-quant-type loops: 2-4 #pragma unroll loops per quant type for loading qs, dm, qh, sc
loop_analysis.notes: Good use of #pragma unroll on most hot loops. The comment at line 1289 explicitly notes that unrolling the outer K loop causes too much register pressure. The load_tiles functions have proper #pragma unroll on their tile-loading loops. However, the inner K loop (line 1290) is NOT unrolled and has a variable trip count (WARP_SIZE/qr/vdr) which is always a compile-time constant but not annotated.

anti_patterns: CRITICAL: No XMX/tensor core compute path — SYCL_USE_XMX define only affects tile sizes, not computation. CUDA has full MMA path for Turing+/CDNA. Intel Xe2 XMX supports int8 joint_matrix but it is completely unused.

CRITICAL: Kernel hardcoded to AMPERE tile sizes — all 10 per-quant kernel functions (mul_mat_q4_0 through mul_mat_q6_K) always use *_AMPERE defines (e.g., MMQ_X_Q4_0_AMPERE, line 1369-1371), ignoring the runtime-selected mmq_x/mmq_y/nwarps from the dispatch function. This is a correctness/performance bug.
HIGH: No stream-K partitioning — CUDA has full stream-K (arxiv 2301.03598) for better SM utilization on small-batch/large-K problems. SYCL uses only conventional 2D tiling.
HIGH: Missing 8 IQ quant types — CUDA supports IQ2_XXS, IQ2_XS, IQ2_S, IQ3_XXS, IQ3_S, IQ1_S, IQ4_NL, IQ4_XS. SYCL only has Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q8_0/Q2_K/Q3_K/Q4_K/Q5_K/Q6_K.
HIGH: No MXFP4 support — CUDA has native FP4 MMA on Blackwell.
MEDIUM: Y data read directly from block_q8_1 in global memory — CUDA pre-reformats into block_q8_1_mmq with transposed/padded layout for conflict-free SLM access.
MEDIUM: SLM bank conflict padding designed for NVIDIA (32 banks × 4B) — Intel Xe2 has 16 banks × 4B, so +1 padding may not be optimal.
MEDIUM: Global barrier (item_ct1.barrier()) used instead of barrier(access::fence_space::local_space) — DPCT artifact, wastes cycles flushing global memory (lines 1287, 1312).
MEDIUM: No [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] on any kernel — compiler may choose SIMD32 reducing occupancy.
LOW: dpct::has_capability_or_fail() called per launch — unnecessary runtime overhead (lines 1818, 1853, etc.).
LOW: dpct::min() instead of sycl::min() or std::min() — DPCT compatibility layer overhead.
LOW: __dpct_inline__ instead of standard inline keyword.
LOW: item_ct1 naming convention (DPCT artifact) throughout ~3000 lines.
LOW: 3D nd_range<3> with first dim=1 for logically 2D work (DPCT artifact).

LOW: Massive code duplication — 10 ggml_mul_mat_*_q8_1_sycl functions are nearly identical (~100 lines each) differing only in quant type and SLM allocation sizes. Should be a single templated function.
LOW: No MoE (Mixture of Experts) support — CUDA has ids_dst/expert_bounds for efficient expert routing.
LOW: No dynamic mmq_x selection — CUDA dynamically picks mmq_x (8-128 in steps of 8) to minimize tiles while fitting in shared memory.

optimization_opportunities.description: Implement Intel XMX (Matrix Extension) compute path using SYCL joint_matrix. The SYCL version uses only dp4a (scalar int8 dot products) despite Intel Xe2 having full XMX hardware support for int8 matrix multiplication. CUDA implements MMA tensor core paths for Turing+ (mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k32.row.col.s32.s8.s8.s32) and AMD CDNA (MFMA). Intel Xe2 supports sycl::ext::oneapi::experimental::joint_matrix with int8 types. The XMX path would perform 8×16 int8 matrix multiplies per cycle vs 4 int8 dp4a operations, yielding ~4x theoretical throughput increase for the compute-bound inner loop.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 3-5x throughput for compute-bound quantized matmul (the most performance-critical operation in LLM inference). XMX provides 8x peak INT8 throughput vs ALU dp4a. Real-world improvement depends on data loading efficiency and SLM utilization.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Define joint_matrix tile types matching Xe2 capabilities: A(m=8,k=32,int8_t), B(k=32,n=16,int8_t), C(m=8,n=16,int32_t). 2. Create new MMA-optimized SLM layout with padding for 128-bit conflict-free access (similar to CUDA's MMQ_MMA_TILE_X_K pattern). 3. Implement load_tiles_mma variant that dequantizes to int8 during SLM loading. 4. Replace the innermost vec_dot loop (line 1290) with joint_matrix::mad() calls. 5. Create new mmq_write_back_mma for the accumulator-to-global writeback. This is a large undertaking (~1000+ lines) but follows the same architectural pattern as CUDA's MMA path.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Major architectural change. joint_matrix API is still maturing in Intel's DPC++ compiler. Requires careful SLM layout design and extensive testing across all 10 quant types. The existing dp4a path should be preserved as fallback.

optimization_opportunities.description: Fix the tile size mismatch bug between dispatch and kernel. The host dispatch functions (ggml_mul_mat_q*_q8_1_sycl) select tile sizes based on compute_capability (VER_GEN13/GEN12/GEN9/VER_4VEC) and compute grid dimensions from them (lines 1785-1807). But the kernel functions (mul_mat_q4_0 etc.) are hardcoded to use *_AMPERE tile sizes (lines 1369-1371). When cc >= VER_GEN12, the dispatch uses RDNA1 tile sizes for the grid but the kernel uses AMPERE tile sizes — which will compute incorrect output tiles or cause out-of-bounds SLM access since SLM is allocated based on dispatch sizes but kernel accesses with AMPERE sizes.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Correctness fix. May also improve performance if non-AMPERE tile sizes are better tuned for the hardware. For Intel Arc Pro B60, the compute capability maps to VER_GEN9 so the current AMPERE path is likely taken consistently, meaning this is probably not hit in practice on this specific GPU — but it's a latent bug for newer hardware.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Make the per-quant kernel functions (mul_mat_q4_0 etc.) use template parameters or runtime parameters for mmq_x, mmq_y, nwarps instead of hardcoded AMPERE constants. 2. Alternatively, define a single set of tile sizes for Intel GPUs (currently the RDNA/PASCAL defines are dead code from the DPCT migration of AMD/NVIDIA constants). 3. Remove the cc-based dispatch entirely and use a single Intel-optimized tile size set. The cleanest fix: template the kernel on mmq_x, mmq_y, nwarps and instantiate for the Intel-optimal values.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Touching tile size logic requires careful verification that SLM allocations match kernel access patterns. Currently the kernel hardcodes AMPERE values and the host allocates SLM based on runtime-selected values — if these don't match, SLM overflows cause silent corruption.

optimization_opportunities.description: Tune tile sizes for Intel Xe2 architecture. The current AMPERE tile sizes (e.g., mmq_x=4, mmq_y=32, nwarps=4 for XMX path; mmq_x=64, mmq_y=128, nwarps=4 for non-XMX) were copied from NVIDIA Ampere GPU tuning. Intel Xe2 has different SLM size (64KB vs 48KB on Ampere), different register file, different SIMD width (16 vs 32), and different memory subsystem. The XMX tile sizes (4×32) are especially problematic — they were designed for NVIDIA tensor cores with warp_size=32, but Intel XMX has different granularity. Optimal tile sizes for Xe2 dp4a path should be determined through benchmarking.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 20-50% throughput improvement from properly tuned tile sizes. The current 4×32 XMX tile sizes produce very small work per work-group (128 output elements) which doesn't amortize SLM loading overhead. For dp4a, 64×64 or 128×64 with 8 sub-groups may be better on Xe2.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Create a new set of Intel Xe2-specific tile size defines (MMQ_X_Q4_0_XE2, etc.). 2. For dp4a path: start with mmq_x=64, mmq_y=64, nwarps=8 (matching 128*16=2048 SIMD lanes on 20 Xe-cores). 3. For XMX path: use joint_matrix granularity (m=8, n=16, k=32) to determine mmq_x/mmq_y — e.g., mmq_x=64 (4 XMX tiles wide), mmq_y=64 (8 XMX tiles tall). 4. Benchmark across all 10 quant types with representative model shapes. 5. The nwarps should be ceil(mmq_y/WARP_SIZE) = ceil(mmq_y/16) for SIMD16.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Only changes dispatch constants — no algorithmic change. Requires benchmarking to find optimal values.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add stream-K work distribution. CUDA implements stream-K partitioning (arxiv 2301.03598) for better EU utilization on small-batch/large-K problems. Stream-K maps a 1D index over all tiles × K-blocks, allowing each work-group to process a contiguous range — potentially splitting a tile's K-reduction across work-groups with a fixup pass. This eliminates the 'tile quantization' problem where some EUs sit idle when the grid doesn't divide evenly across compute units.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 15-40% throughput improvement for small batch sizes (1-8 tokens) where conventional tiling severely underutilizes the 20 Xe-cores. For example, with mmq_y=128 and a 4096-row weight matrix, only 32 tiles exist in the X dimension — barely enough to keep 20 Xe-cores busy. Stream-K would distribute the K-dimension work more evenly.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Implement the stream-K kernel variant: map a 1D index kbc over all (tile_x, tile_y, k_block) combinations. 2. Each work-group processes floor(total_kbc / n_groups) or ceil() blocks contiguously. 3. When a work-group's range spans two tiles, it writes partial results to a fixup buffer. 4. Launch a second kernel (mul_mat_q_stream_k_fixup) to sum partial results. 5. Fall back to conventional tiling when ntiles > n_xe_cores * 2 (stream-K overhead not worth it). Reference: CUDA mmq.cuh lines 3459-3750.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Adds a second kernel launch and requires a temporary fixup buffer. The fixup kernel is simple (element-wise addition). Main risk is getting the tile boundary conditions correct.

optimization_opportunities.description: Optimize Y data loading with pre-formatted block_q8_1_mmq layout. CUDA pre-reformats Y (query/activation) data into a custom block_q8_1_mmq struct with transposed, padded layout optimized for conflict-free SLM access. The SYCL version reads Y data directly from standard block_q8_1 structs in global memory on every K sub-iteration, causing redundant global memory traffic and suboptimal SLM access patterns.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-25% throughput improvement from reduced global memory traffic and conflict-free SLM access for Y data. Currently each qr sub-iteration re-reads Y data from global memory; with pre-formatting, the entire Y tile can be loaded once and reused.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Define a SYCL equivalent of block_q8_1_mmq with 128 int8 values + 16 bytes scales per tile block. 2. Create a reformatting kernel or host-side preparation step. 3. Modify the mul_mat_q inner loop to load Y from the reformatted buffer. 4. Adjust tile_y_qs and tile_y_ds SLM layouts to match the new format.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires changes to the Y data pipeline outside mmq.cpp. The reformatting has a cost that must be amortized across multiple matmul calls.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to all kernel launches and replace global barriers with local barriers. All 20 kernel launches (10 quant types × 2 need_check variants) lack the sub-group size attribute. On Xe2, the compiler may choose SIMD32 which halves the number of hardware threads and reduces occupancy. Additionally, all 2 barriers per K-iteration (lines 1287, 1312) use the default global fence instead of access::fence_space::local_space — wasteful since only SLM is accessed between barriers.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% throughput improvement from guaranteed SIMD16 selection and reduced barrier cost. The barrier improvement is especially significant since it's called 2×qr times per K-tile (up to 16 times for Q5_K).
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Add [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to each cgh.parallel_for lambda. 2. Replace item_ct1.barrier() with item_ct1.barrier(sycl::access::fence_space::local_space) at lines 1287 and 1312. 3. Note: WARP_SIZE is currently 32 (presets.hpp:19) but Xe2 native SIMD is 16. The kernel logic uses WARP_SIZE=32 as the tile K dimension and for SLM addressing — this is independent of the actual SIMD width and should continue to work with reqd_sub_group_size(16), where 2 sub-groups form one logical 'warp'.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: reqd_sub_group_size(16) is a compiler hint. barrier(local_space) is a strict subset of the default barrier. Both are safe changes.

optimization_opportunities.description: Eliminate massive code duplication by templating the dispatch functions. The 10 ggml_mul_mat_*_q8_1_sycl functions (lines 1773-2960) are nearly identical ~100-line functions differing only in quant type, SLM tile variable names, and SLM allocation sizes. This can be reduced to a single templated dispatch function, improving maintainability and reducing binary size.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: No runtime improvement — pure code quality. Reduces ~1200 lines to ~120 lines. Makes future changes (tile size tuning, XMX path, stream-K) much easier to implement since they only need to be added once.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Create a template function template<typename block_q_t, int qk, int qr, int qi, bool need_sum, auto alloc_fn, auto load_fn, int vdr, auto dot_fn> ggml_mul_mat_q_sycl(). 2. Compute SLM sizes from template parameters using a traits struct similar to CUDA's mmq_type_traits. 3. Replace all 10 functions with instantiations of the template.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Pure refactoring — no algorithmic change. Must verify SLM allocation sizes match the original per-quant calculations.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add support for missing IQ quant types. CUDA supports 8 additional IQ (importance quantization) types: IQ2_XXS, IQ2_XS, IQ2_S, IQ3_XXS, IQ3_S, IQ1_S, IQ4_NL, IQ4_XS. These are used by highly compressed models (2-3 bit quantization) and are increasingly popular. The SYCL mmq kernel only supports 10 basic quant types.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Feature completeness — enables running IQ-quantized models on Intel GPUs via the MMQ path. Performance impact depends on model usage patterns. IQ types are increasingly common for edge deployment.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Implement allocate_tiles_iq*, load_tiles_iq*, vec_dot_iq*_q8_1_mul_mat for each IQ type following the pattern of existing quant types. 2. Add dispatch cases in ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat_q (line 2987). 3. Reference: CUDA mmq.cuh mmq_type_traits specializations for IQ types. 4. This is substantial work (~200 lines per IQ type) but follows established patterns.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: IQ types have complex dequantization (lookup tables, variable block sizes). Must match CUDA implementations exactly for numerical correctness.

optimization_opportunities.description: Clean up DPCT migration artifacts. Remove dpct::has_capability_or_fail() calls (10+ occurrences), replace __dpct_inline__ with inline, replace dpct::min() with sycl::min() or std::min(), rename item_ct1 to item, convert nd_range<3> to nd_range<2> (since first dim is always 1), remove DPCT warning comments (20+ occurrences of DPCT1049, DPCT1065, DPCT1110, DPCT1118).
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Minor runtime improvement from removing dpct::has_capability_or_fail() per-launch overhead. Primary benefit is code clarity — the file has ~50 DPCT comments cluttering 3000 lines.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Mechanical search-and-replace across the entire file. The dpct::has_capability_or_fail removal is the most impactful — it does a synchronous device query per kernel launch.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Purely mechanical refactoring.

kernels.estimated_current_efficiency: 15-25% — The MMQ kernel is the most performance-critical kernel in LLM inference (dominating token generation time), yet the SYCL version is severely underperforming: no XMX/tensor core compute (using dp4a at ~1/4 theoretical peak INT8 throughput), hardcoded NVIDIA tile sizes, no stream-K for small batches, suboptimal Y data loading, missing IQ quant types, tile size mismatch bug between dispatch and kernel, and pervasive DPCT artifacts. The missing XMX path alone represents a 3-5x potential improvement.

kernels.name: mmvq (quantized matrix-vector multiply) SYCL kernels

launch_config.work_group_size: Non-reorder path: WARP_SIZE (16 on Intel) in dimension 2, GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y (1) in dimension 1 — total work-group size = 16. Reorder path: num_subgroups*WARP_SIZE (16*16=256) in dimension 2, GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y (1) in dimension 1 — total work-group size = 256.
launch_config.global_size_expression: Non-reorder: nd_range<3>((1,1,block_num_y) * (1,GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y,WARP_SIZE)) where block_num_y = ceil(nrows/GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y). Reorder: nd_range<3>((1,GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y,block_num_y*WARP_SIZE), (1,GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y,num_subgroups*WARP_SIZE)). One sub-group per row.
launch_config.notes: CRITICAL: Non-reorder path has an effective work-group size of only 16 (1 sub-group). This is catastrophically small for Xe2 — only 1 hardware thread per XVE, minimal latency hiding. CUDA uses 4 warps (nwarps=4, 128 threads total for ncols_dst<=4) to process multiple rows per block and performs inter-warp SLM reduction. The reorder path is much better at 256 threads (16 sub-groups). All non-reorder launches correctly have [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]]. 3D nd_range with dim 0 always 1 (DPCT artifact).

memory_patterns.notes: Adjacent lanes within a sub-group access adjacent quantized blocks along the K dimension — this is coalesced for row-major weight layout. Y data (block_q8_1) is accessed via pointer arithmetic with sequential offsets — coalesced. No sycl::vec usage for loading quantized data. The reorder path uses a custom reordered block layout (get_block_offset, get_d_offset) designed for better memory access patterns on Intel GPUs. Non-reorder path casts vx to block_q_t* with AOS layout, which may cause non-coalesced access for scale/quantized data interleaving in K-quant types.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM usage in any SYCL mmvq kernel. CUDA uses __shared__ tmp_shared[nwarps-1][ncols_dst][rows_per_block][warp_size] for inter-warp partial sum reduction. The SYCL version avoids SLM by using only 1 sub-group per row, but this trades off occupancy for simplicity. The reorder path uses sycl::reduce_over_group which is SLM-free (sub-group shuffle only).

reduction_pattern.notes: TWO inconsistent reduction patterns: (1) Reorder path (mul_mat_vec_q_reorder, line 52) correctly uses sycl::reduce_over_group(sub_group, partial_sum, plus<>()) — clean, modern SYCL. (2) Non-reorder path (mul_mat_vec_q + all 9 IQ variants, lines 93-96) uses manual dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor shuffle reduction — a DPCT migration artifact. The manual reduction is functionally correct but generates more instructions and is harder to maintain. The reorder path is the model for how all kernels should be written.

data_types.notes: FP32 accumulation throughout, which is appropriate for dot product precision. Y data uses block_q8_1 (int8 quantized with half2 scale/min). X data varies by quant type. joint_matrix is not applicable to matvec (it's for matmul tiles).

functions: vec_dot_q*_q8_1 (type-specific dot product functions from vecdotq.hpp)
math_functions.notes: No transcendental math — purely integer arithmetic (dp4a, bitwise ops, shifts) in the vec_dot functions. The computational core is in vecdotq.hpp which is shared with mmq. The reorder path uses separate vecdotq functions optimized for the reordered memory layout.

hot_loops: Non-reorder outer loop (line 79): for (i = lid/(qi/vdr); i < blocks_per_row; i += blocks_per_warp) — iterates blocks_per_row/blocks_per_warp times
Non-reorder inner loop (line 84): for (elem = 0; elem < qi/vdr; elem += WARP_SIZE) — typically 0 or 1 iterations since qi/vdr is often <= WARP_SIZE
Reorder outer loop (line 33): for (i = lid/block_elements_per_subgroup; i < blocks_per_row; i += blocks_per_subgroup) — iterates blocks_per_row/blocks_per_subgroup times
Reorder inner loop (line 44): #pragma unroll for (elem = 0; elem < block_elements_per_subgroup; elem += WARP_SIZE) — compile-time constant, properly unrolled
Dispatch loop (line 1062): for (i = 0; i < src1_ncols; i++) — iterates over output columns sequentially on the HOST — one kernel launch per column
loop_analysis.notes: The reorder path correctly uses #pragma unroll on its inner loop (line 43). Non-reorder path inner loops lack #pragma unroll but have small trip counts (often 1). The CRITICAL issue is the HOST-side dispatch loop (line 1062) launching one kernel per output column — CUDA processes up to 8 columns per kernel launch using ncols_dst template parameter with shared memory reduction.

anti_patterns: CRITICAL: Host-side column loop (line 1062) launches one kernel per output column — CUDA batches up to 8 columns per launch via ncols_dst template parameter with inter-warp SLM reduction. For batch_size=4, this means 4 separate kernel launches vs CUDA's 1, adding 4x kernel launch overhead and 4x redundant weight reads from global memory

The tiny work-group means only 1 hardware thread per XVE, providing minimal memory latency hiding. Increasing to 4 sub-groups (64 threads) with sub-group cooperative reduction would improve throughput 2-3x

LOW: dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor instead of sycl::sub_group::shuffle_xor (DPCT compatibility wrapper)
