optimization_opportunities.description: Implement multi-column batching matching CUDA's ncols_dst template parameter. Currently the host dispatch function (ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat_vec_q, line 1062) loops over src1_ncols and launches a separate kernel per column. CUDA batches up to 8 columns per kernel launch using a compile-time ncols_dst parameter, with each warp computing dot products for all ncols_dst columns simultaneously using register-level accumulation (float tmp[ncols_dst][rows_per_block]) and a single SLM-based inter-warp reduction at the end. This eliminates redundant weight reads — the same quantized weight block is dotted with ncols_dst different Y vectors in a single load.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2-4x throughput for small batch sizes (2-8 tokens). For batch_size=4, reduces kernel launches from 4 to 1, eliminates 3 redundant weight reads from global memory (the dominant cost for this memory-bound kernel), and reduces dispatch overhead. Weight matrix memory traffic drops from batch_size * matrix_bytes to 1 * matrix_bytes.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Template mul_mat_vec_q on ncols_dst (1-8). 2. Each sub-group accumulates float tmp[ncols_dst] — multiple dot products per weight load. 3. Inner loop: for each kbx, load the weight block once, then dot with ncols_dst Y vectors: for (j=0; j<ncols_dst; j++) tmp[j] += vec_dot(x_block, y[j*stride+kby], iqs). 4. Replace host-side for loop with a switch on src1_ncols dispatching to the correct template instantiation. 5. For ncols_dst >= 2, use nwarps=2 (32 threads) with SLM inter-warp reduction matching CUDA's pattern: __shared__ tmp_shared[nwarps-1][ncols_dst][warp_size]. 6. Apply to both generic and IQ kernel variants.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Moderate complexity — requires SLM allocation for inter-warp reduction and careful stride management for Y vector offsets. CUDA's implementation is well-tested and can serve as reference. Register pressure increases with ncols_dst but is manageable (8 floats per thread for ncols_dst=8).

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase non-reorder work-group size from WARP_SIZE (16) to at least 64 (4 sub-groups) with inter-sub-group cooperative reduction. Currently each non-reorder kernel launch has a work-group of only 16 threads (1 sub-group). On Xe2, this uses only 1 of 8 possible hardware threads per XVE, providing minimal memory latency hiding. CUDA uses nwarps=4 (128 threads) for batch_size <= 4 and nwarps=2 for batch_size 5-8. Increasing to 4 sub-groups (64 threads on Xe2's SIMD16) would allow 4 hardware threads to cooperate on each row, splitting the K-dimension work and reducing per-row latency.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2-3x throughput for the non-reorder path. More hardware threads per work-group improves memory latency hiding (the #1 performance factor for this memory-bound kernel). Combined with multi-column batching, this could yield 4-8x total improvement.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Change block_dims from (1, GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y, WARP_SIZE) to (1, GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y, nwarps*WARP_SIZE) where nwarps = 4 for ncols_dst<=4, 2 for ncols_dst 5-8. 2. Each sub-group computes a partial sum over blocks_per_row / nwarps blocks. 3. After the K-loop, write non-leader sub-group partial sums to SLM: float slm[nwarps-1][WARP_SIZE]. 4. Barrier. 5. Leader sub-group reads and accumulates partial sums, then reduces within sub-group. 6. Only thread 0 writes dst[row]. This exactly matches CUDA's multi-warp reduction pattern.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Well-established pattern — matches CUDA's nwarps approach. SLM usage is minimal (< 256 bytes per work-group for nwarps=4). The reorder path already achieves this with 16 sub-groups.

optimization_opportunities.description: Consolidate 11 nearly identical kernel functions into a single unified template. The generic mul_mat_vec_q and 9 IQ-specific variants (iq2_xxs, iq2_xs, iq2_s, iq3_xxs, iq3_s, iq1_s, iq1_m, iq4_nl, iq4_xs) are each 40-50 lines with identical structure, differing only in the vec_dot function called and extra parameters (lookup table pointers). CUDA unifies everything into a single template using constexpr get_vec_dot_q_cuda(type) dispatch. Similarly, the 20+ dispatch functions are boilerplate copies. This duplication means any optimization (multi-column, multi-warp, etc.) must be replicated 11+20=31 times.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: No direct performance improvement — code quality and maintainability. Reduces ~900 lines of kernels + ~500 lines of dispatchers to ~100+50 lines. Makes all other optimizations (multi-column, multi-warp, fusion) far cheaper to implement since they only need to be done once.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Create a single template kernel: template<ggml_type type> mul_mat_vec_q_unified(...). 2. Use constexpr switch/if to select vec_dot function, qk, qi, vdr, and any lookup table pointers at compile time. Define a traits struct per quant type following CUDA's pattern. 3. For IQ types that need extra parameters (grid tables, sign tables), pass them as template-selected constexpr pointers. 4. Create a single dispatch function: template<ggml_type type> mul_mat_vec_q_sycl_dispatch(vx, vy, dst, ncols, nrows, stream) that handles all quant types. 5. The dispatch switch in ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat_vec_q (line 1066) remains but each case calls the single template instead of a per-type function.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Pure refactoring. The kernel logic for each quant type is identical — the only variations are in the vec_dot function signature (some pass extra lookup table params). These can be handled with template specialization or constexpr if.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add GLU fusion support matching CUDA's has_fusion template parameter. CUDA fuses gate matrix multiplication + bias addition + GLU activation (swiglu, geglu, swiglu_oai) into the mmvq kernel. For each row, the kernel simultaneously computes dot(weight, y) and dot(gate, y), applies bias, then applies the GLU activation — all in a single kernel launch with shared Y data. Without fusion, SYCL requires 3+ separate kernel launches (gate mmvq + bias add + GLU), each reading/writing the full output tensor.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 30-50% throughput improvement for models using GLU activations (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, and most modern LLMs). Eliminates 2+ kernel launches and 4+ extra global memory passes (2 reads + 2 writes for bias and GLU).
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Add a has_fusion template parameter to mul_mat_vec_q. 2. When has_fusion=true, accept additional parameters: gate pointer, x_bias pointer, gate_bias pointer, glu_op enum. 3. In the K-loop, compute tmp_gate[j] += vec_dot(vgate, y, ...) alongside tmp[j] += vec_dot(vx, y, ...). 4. After reduction, apply: result = tmp + x_bias; gate_val = tmp_gate + gate_bias; result = glu_op(result, gate_val). 5. The gate weight matrix has the same quantization type and layout as the main weight — reuses the same vec_dot functions. 6. Add ggml_cuda_mm_fusion_args equivalent struct for SYCL dispatch. Requires integration with the SYCL backend op dispatch in ggml-sycl.cpp.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires changes to both the kernel and the dispatch layer (ggml-sycl.cpp must detect fusible patterns and pass fusion parameters). Register pressure doubles (accumulating both x and gate results). The CUDA implementation is well-documented and can serve as reference.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace manual dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor shuffle reduction with sycl::reduce_over_group in all non-reorder kernels. The reorder path (mul_mat_vec_q_reorder, line 52) already correctly uses sycl::reduce_over_group(sub_group, partial_sum, plus<>()). But the generic mul_mat_vec_q (lines 93-96) and all 9 IQ variants use a manual 4-step XOR shuffle loop — a DPCT migration artifact that generates suboptimal code. The inconsistency between the two paths means the codebase has two different reduction implementations for the same operation.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-10% throughput from better code generation. sycl::reduce_over_group gives the compiler full visibility into the reduction pattern, enabling optimal instruction selection (potentially using hardware-native reduction when available). Also eliminates the DPCT dependency on dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace lines 93-96 (and equivalent in all 9 IQ variants) from: #pragma unroll for (int mask = WARP_SIZE/2; mask > 0; mask >>= 1) { tmp += dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor(item_ct1.get_sub_group(), tmp, mask); } if (item_ct1.get_local_id(2) == 0) { dst[row] = tmp; } TO: auto sum = sycl::reduce_over_group(item_ct1.get_sub_group(), tmp, std::plus<>()); if (item_ct1.get_sub_group().leader()) { dst[row] = sum; }
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The reorder path already proves sycl::reduce_over_group works correctly for this exact use case. Strictly equivalent functional change.

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y from 1 to 2 to process 2 rows per work-group. CUDA uses rows_per_cuda_block=2 for ncols_dst >= 2, amortizing thread setup and reduction overhead across 2 rows. The SYCL work-group Y dimension (GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y) controls how many rows are processed — currently fixed at 1. With GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y=2, each work-group processes 2 adjacent rows, halving the number of work-groups launched (reducing kernel dispatch grid overhead) and improving data locality for weight matrix reads.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-20% throughput from better row amortization. Each sub-group still processes one row independently, but 2 rows share the same work-group, improving scheduling efficiency and reducing grid overhead. The benefit is larger for small nrows (where grid efficiency matters most).
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Change GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y from 1 to 2 in presets.hpp (line 61). 2. Verify that block_num_y = ceil(nrows / GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y) correctly handles odd nrows. 3. The kernel already indexes via item.get_local_id(1) for the Y dimension — with GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y=2, two rows are processed per work-group. 4. The early-return guard (if row >= nrows) handles the last work-group when nrows is odd. 5. Note: this effectively doubles the work-group size from 16 to 32 (or 256 to 512 for reorder), which may affect occupancy — benchmark to verify.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The kernel already supports GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y > 1 by design (the row index computation uses local_range(1) and local_id(1)). The only risk is occupancy reduction from doubling work-group size, which should be tested.

optimization_opportunities.description: Fix reorder path assertion that block_num_y must be divisible by num_subgroups. Lines 542, 767, and 811 have GGML_ASSERT(block_num_y % num_subgroups == 0) where num_subgroups=16. This means the reorder path crashes if ceil(nrows / GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y) is not divisible by 16. For models with nrows not a multiple of 16 (or 32 with MMV_Y=2), the reorder path cannot be used. CUDA's equivalent code has no such restriction — it simply uses an early-return guard.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Correctness fix — enables the reorder path (which is 2-3x faster than non-reorder) for all model dimensions.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1. Remove the GGML_ASSERT(block_num_y % num_subgroups == 0). 2. Change global_size calculation from block_num_y * WARP_SIZE to ceil_div(block_num_y, num_subgroups) * num_subgroups * WARP_SIZE (pad the grid up to a multiple of the work-group size). 3. The kernel already has if (row >= nrows) return guard (line 20), so excess work-items safely exit. 4. This is the same approach used by the non-reorder path and by CUDA.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The kernel already handles excess rows via early return. Padding the grid is standard practice.

optimization_opportunities.description: Clean up DPCT artifacts: convert 3D nd_range to 2D (dim 0 is always 1), replace dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor with sycl::sub_group shuffle (covered by opt_009_005), replace item_ct1 naming with item, replace get_local_id(2)/get_group(2) with get_local_id(0)/get_group(0) after ndim reduction.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: No performance impact — code quality. Simplifies 20+ kernel launches and 10+ kernel functions.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Mechanical search-and-replace across mmvq.cpp. The 3D -> 2D conversion changes nd_range<3>((1,Y,X), (1,Y,X)) to nd_range<2>((Y,X), (Y,X)) and nd_item<3> to nd_item<2>.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Purely mechanical refactoring. No algorithmic changes.

kernels.estimated_current_efficiency: 25-35% — The mmvq kernel is the most performance-critical kernel for single-token generation (autoregressive decode), yet the SYCL version has several major gaps vs CUDA: (1) one kernel launch per output column instead of batching up to 8, causing redundant weight reads; (2) work-group size of only 16 threads for the non-reorder path (CUDA uses 128), providing minimal memory latency hiding; (3) no GLU fusion, requiring 3+ extra kernel launches for GLU models; (4) massive code duplication across 31 functions making optimization expensive. The reorder path (available for Q4_0, Q4_K, Q6_K) is much better designed — 256 threads, sycl::reduce_over_group, proper unrolling — but only covers 3 of 20 quant types. The non-reorder path serving the other 17 quant types is severely underperforming.

kernels.name: dmmv (dequantize matrix-vector multiply) SYCL kernels

launch_config.work_group_size: Generic template (Q4_0..Q8_0, F16): WARP_SIZE (16 on Intel) in dim 2, GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y (1) in dim 1 — total 16 threads. Reorder path (Q4_0 only): same as generic, 16 threads. K-quant kernels (Q2_K..Q6_K): QK_WARP_SIZE (32) in dim 2, ny (1 or 2) in dim 1 — total 32 or 64 threads. Q5_K special: 1 row per work-group, QK_WARP_SIZE (32) threads. All are catastrophically small for Intel Xe2.
launch_config.sub_group_size: Mixed: generic template uses [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]] = 16. K-quant kernels use [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(QK_WARP_SIZE)]] = 32 (forces SIMD32 on Intel, reducing occupancy).
launch_config.global_size_expression: Generic: nd_range<3>((1,1,block_num_y) * (1,GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y,WARP_SIZE)) where block_num_y = ceil(nrows/GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y). K-quant: nd_range<3>((1,1,block_num_y) * (1,ny,QK_WARP_SIZE)). Q5_K: nd_range<3>((1,1,nrows) * (1,1,QK_WARP_SIZE)).
launch_config.notes: CRITICAL: All kernels have tiny work-groups (16-64 threads). The CUDA counterpart (mmvf.cu) dynamically selects block_size from 32 to 256 based on ncols, uses up to 8 warps per block with SLM inter-warp reduction, and processes up to 8 output columns per kernel launch. The SYCL dmmv processes only 1 row per work-group with 1 sub-group (16 threads for basic quants, 32 for K-quants). GGML_SYCL_DMMV_X=32 means each thread processes 2*32/16=4 values per outer iteration. With 16 threads, the entire work-group processes only 64 quantized values per iteration — extremely low utilization on Xe2 where each XVE has 8 hardware threads. 3D nd_range with dim 0 always 1 (DPCT artifact).

strided_accesses: K-quant kernels (Q2_K..Q6_K) access y[] with strides of 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112, 128 — non-contiguous and non-coalesced across sub-group lanes
K-quant kernels access block_q*_K fields (qs, scales, hmask, qh) with irregular strides depending on the quant-type specific indexing pattern
memory_patterns.notes: Generic template: Adjacent threads access adjacent blocks along K — coalesced. Dequantize function reads 2 values at a time (dfloat2), but not using sycl::vec. Y data is accessed sequentially per thread. K-quant kernels: Weight data accessed via AOS block layout (block_q2_K, etc.) with per-block scale/quant interleaving — inherently not vectorizable. Y data accessed with large strides (y[l+0], y[l+32], y[l+64], ...) within each thread — cache-unfriendly. CUDA uses float2 vectorized loads (y2 pointer) for Y data; SYCL uses scalar float loads throughout.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM usage in any dmmv kernel. CUDA uses shared memory (buf_iw[]) for inter-warp reduction when block_size > warp_size. The SYCL version avoids SLM by using only 1 sub-group per work-group, but this eliminates the ability to use larger work-groups with multi-sub-group cooperative reduction.

reduction_pattern.notes: ALL kernels use manual dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor shuffle reduction — a DPCT migration artifact. Generic template: reduces with mask_start = WARP_SIZE>>1 or WARP_SIZE>>2 depending on ncols vs GGML_SYCL_DMMV_X. K-quant kernels: reduces with QK_WARP_SIZE/2 iterations (5 steps for 32-wide). Should use sycl::reduce_over_group(sub_group, tmp, sycl::plus<>()) for cleaner, potentially faster code. The reorder path (dequantize_mul_mat_vec_reorder) also uses the same dpct shuffle reduction — unlike mmvq's reorder path which correctly uses sycl::reduce_over_group.

data_types.compute_type: float (or half2 when GGML_SYCL_F16 is defined, but this is typically not enabled)
data_types.notes: GGML_SYCL_F16 path exists for basic quants (Q4_0..Q8_0, F16) using sycl::half2 accumulation, but it is typically not compiled in. K-quant kernels always use FP32 accumulation regardless of GGML_SYCL_F16 — no half2 path. CUDA uses half2 accumulation when precision allows, giving 2x compute throughput on half-capable hardware. joint_matrix not applicable to matvec operations.

functions: dequantize_q4_0, dequantize_q4_1, dequantize_q5_0, dequantize_q5_1, dequantize_q8_0, convert_f16, convert_f32 (inline dequantize functions)
dpct::has_capability_or_fail (runtime capability check on basic quant launchers)
math_functions.notes: No transcendental math — purely integer arithmetic (bit shifts, masks) and FP multiply-add. The computational core is in the dequantize_kernel functions (from dequantize.hpp) which extract values from packed quantized formats. K-quant kernels inline the dequantization directly with extensive bit manipulation. No FMA intrinsics used — relies on compiler optimization for multiply-add fusion.

hot_loops: Generic template outer K loop (line 47): for (i = 0; i < ncols; i += iter_stride) where iter_stride = 2*GGML_SYCL_DMMV_X = 64. Iterates ncols/64 times. Each iteration processes vals_per_iter=4 quantized values per thread.
Generic template inner unrolled loop (line 55): #pragma unroll for (j = 0; j < vals_per_iter; j += 2) — processes 2 values per iteration, 2 iterations total for vals_per_iter=4.
K-quant outer block loop (e.g., Q2_K line 266): for (i = ix; i < num_blocks_per_row; i += K_QUANTS_PER_ITERATION) — iterates num_blocks_per_row/2 times.
K-quant inner value loop (e.g., Q2_K line 281): for (l = 0; l < K_QUANTS_PER_ITERATION; ++l) — 1 or 2 iterations, accumulates 8 products per iteration for Q2_K.
Reduction loop (all kernels): for (mask = start; mask > 0; mask >>= 1) — log2(sub_group_size) iterations (4 or 5 steps).
Reorder path has 2 copies of main loop body — aligned path (line 122) and residual path (line 152)
loop_analysis.notes: Generic template inner loop properly #pragma unrolled. K-quant inner loops have very small trip counts (1-2) so unrolling is implicit. Reduction loops are #pragma unrolled. The reorder path duplicates the entire loop body for the aligned vs residual tail case — significant code duplication. No loop over output columns (always 1 output per work-group row).

anti_patterns: CRITICAL: Work-group sizes are catastrophically small — 16 threads for basic quants, 32-64 for K-quants. CUDA uses 32-256 threads with dynamic selection based on ncols. On Xe2 with 16-wide SIMD, a 16-thread work-group means only 1 hardware thread per XVE — 7 of 8 hardware threads are idle, providing almost zero memory latency hiding. Increasing to 128-256 threads (8-16 sub-groups) with SLM-based inter-sub-group reduction would improve throughput 4-8x for memory-bound kernels.

CRITICAL: QK_WARP_SIZE=32 mismatch with Intel WARP_SIZE=16 — K-quant kernels (Q2_K through Q6_K) use reqd_sub_group_size(QK_WARP_SIZE) = reqd_sub_group_size(32), forcing SIMD32 mode on Intel. This reduces occupancy compared to SIMD16. More importantly, the K-quant kernel indexing logic (tid = local_id(2)/K_QUANTS_PER_ITERATION) was designed for 32 CUDA threads and may produce incorrect results or underutilize lanes when forced into SIMD32 on non-NVIDIA hardware. Additionally, the reduction uses QK_WARP_SIZE/2 = 16 as the start mask, which requires exactly 32-wide sub-groups.

HIGH: Only processes 1 output column per kernel launch — CUDA processes up to 8 columns per block (ncols_dst template parameter), amortizing weight reads across columns. For batch_size=4, SYCL launches 4 separate kernels while CUDA uses 1, eliminating 3/4 of redundant global memory reads.

HIGH: No multi-row processing — GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y=1 for basic quants (K-quants use ny=2 for Q2_K/Q3_K/Q4_K/Q6_K but not Q5_K). CUDA dynamically adjusts rows per block. Processing 2-4 rows per work-group with the same weight data would improve weight reuse and reduce grid overhead.

HIGH: Massive code duplication — K-quant kernels (Q2_K through Q6_K) are each 100-200 lines of hand-written per-quant-type code, totaling ~620 lines. The generic template handles basic quants in 90 lines. The 11 _sycl dispatch functions (lines 867-1071) are nearly identical boilerplate (15-25 lines each). CUDA has replaced all of this with a single unified mul_mat_vec_f template that handles all float types with vectorized loads.

MEDIUM: All dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor shuffle reductions should use sycl::reduce_over_group — generates more optimal code and is the correct SYCL idiom. The mmvq reorder path already uses reduce_over_group correctly.

MEDIUM: No vectorized Y loads — CUDA uses float2 (y2 pointer) for coalesced 64-bit Y data access. SYCL K-quant kernels access y[] with scalar loads at various strides (y[l+0], y[l+16], y[l+32], etc.), causing poor cache behavior.

MEDIUM: No GLU/bias fusion — CUDA mmvf.cu has full has_fusion template parameter for fused gate matmul + bias + GLU activation (swiglu, geglu). SYCL dmmv has no fusion support at all, requiring 3+ extra kernel launches for fused models.

MEDIUM: dpct::has_capability_or_fail() called on every launch of basic quant kernels (Q4_0..Q8_0, F16) — checking fp16 capability at runtime is unnecessary overhead since the capability was already verified at initialization.
LOW: K-quant kernels Q2_K, Q3_K, Q6_K have off-by-one boundary check: 'if (row > nrows)' should be 'if (row >= nrows)' — potential out-of-bounds write for the last row.
LOW: Reorder path duplicates entire main loop body for aligned vs residual tail (lines 122-150 and 152-181) — should be factored into a helper.
LOW: 3D nd_range<3> with dim 0 always 1 on all launch sites (DPCT artifact).
LOW: DPCT artifacts throughout: item_ct1 naming, dpct::has_capability_or_fail, dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor, __dpct_inline__ on dequantize functions.

LOW: GGML_SYCL_F16 half2 path is dead code for K-quants — K-quant kernels always use float regardless of GGML_SYCL_F16, so the compile-time flag provides no benefit for the most important quant types (Q4_K, Q6_K).
LOW: Missing BF16 support — CUDA mmvf.cu handles nv_bfloat16 natively. SYCL dmmv has no BF16 path, so BF16 models must use a different (likely slower) path.

kernels.estimated_current_efficiency: 20-30% — The dmmv kernel handles the fallback case for dequantize-and-multiply matvec when the mmvq quantized path is not used (e.g., for basic quants on Intel where GGML_SYCL_PRIORITIZE_DMMV controls routing). It is severely hampered by tiny work-group sizes (16-64 threads vs CUDA's 32-256), complete lack of multi-column batching (1 column per launch vs CUDA's 8), QK_WARP_SIZE=32 forcing SIMD32 on K-quant kernels, no SLM-based inter-sub-group reduction, no vectorized Y loads, no GLU fusion, and ~620 lines of duplicated K-quant code. The reorder path for Q4_0 is slightly better but still uses only 16 threads. On Intel Xe2, the memory latency hiding from the tiny work-groups alone limits throughput to perhaps 20-30% of achievable bandwidth.

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase work-group size from 16-32 to 128-256 with multi-sub-group SLM reduction. Currently all kernels use only 1 sub-group (16 or 32 threads), providing minimal memory latency hiding on Xe2. CUDA dynamically selects 32-256 threads with inter-warp SLM reduction. Implementing 8-16 sub-groups per work-group with sycl::reduce_over_group or SLM partial-sum reduction would provide 4-8x throughput improvement for this memory-bound kernel.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 4-8x throughput improvement for memory-bound cases (most common)
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add SLM allocation for inter-sub-group partial sums. Each sub-group computes a partial sum, stores to SLM, barrier, then sub-group 0 reduces the partial sums. Use [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] consistently. This is the same pattern CUDA uses with shared memory buf_iw[]. For K-quant kernels, this requires adapting the indexing from per-warp to per-work-group-chunk.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: K-quant kernel indexing logic is tightly coupled to thread count assumptions. Need to verify index computation still covers all quantized values when distributing across multiple sub-groups. Generic template is lower risk since the loop-stride pattern naturally extends.

optimization_opportunities.description: Fix QK_WARP_SIZE mismatch — K-quant kernels use reqd_sub_group_size(32) via QK_WARP_SIZE on Intel where native SIMD width is 16. This forces SIMD32 mode which halves occupancy. The reduction loop uses QK_WARP_SIZE/2=16 as start mask. Should rewrite K-quant kernels to use WARP_SIZE=16 sub-groups natively, adjusting the indexing arithmetic to distribute work across 16-wide sub-groups instead of 32-wide.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 15-40% occupancy and throughput improvement from using native SIMD16 instead of forced SIMD32
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(QK_WARP_SIZE)]] with [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]]. Recompute tid/ix/step/im/in indexing for 16 threads instead of 32. Adjust reduction mask_start from QK_WARP_SIZE/2 to WARP_SIZE/2. Need to verify all K-quant variants (Q2_K through Q6_K) correctly handle the reduced thread count — some use tid to select 128-value halves (im = tid/step where step = 16/K_QUANTS_PER_ITERATION).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The K-quant indexing logic is complex and was designed for exactly 32 threads. Changing to 16 requires carefully rethinking how each thread covers the 256-element QK_K super-block. Some paths may need K_QUANTS_PER_ITERATION adjustment. Correctness testing required for all 5 K-quant types.

optimization_opportunities.description: Implement multi-column output batching (ncols_dst template parameter). Currently processes 1 output column per kernel launch. CUDA processes up to 8 columns per block, amortizing weight reads. For batch_size=4, this would reduce kernel launches by 4x and eliminate 3/4 of redundant global memory reads of the weight matrix.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2-4x throughput for batch sizes 2-8 (proportional to reduced weight reads)
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add ncols_dst template parameter to the kernel. Accumulate sumf[ncols_dst] partial sums. Load weight data once, multiply by ncols_dst different Y vectors. The caller already receives src1_ncols — use it to select ncols_dst at dispatch time. SLM needed for multi-column inter-sub-group reduction.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Increases register pressure proportionally to ncols_dst. May need to reduce work-group size for large ncols_dst. The existing dispatch infrastructure (ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat) may need changes to pass multiple Y columns.

optimization_opportunities.description: Fix off-by-one boundary check in K-quant kernels Q2_K, Q3_K, Q4_K, Q6_K. They use 'if (row > nrows) return;' which should be 'if (row >= nrows) return;'. With ny=2 and nrows odd, the last work-item will have row == nrows and write to dst[nrows] — an out-of-bounds access. Q5_K does not have this bug (uses different indexing).
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Correctness fix — prevents potential out-of-bounds write and memory corruption
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change 'if (row > nrows)' to 'if (row >= nrows)' in dequantize_mul_mat_vec_q2_k (line 237), dequantize_mul_mat_vec_q3_k (line 361), dequantize_mul_mat_vec_q4_k (line 480), dequantize_mul_mat_vec_q6_k (line 759).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Simple one-character fix. May currently be masked by row padding (MATRIX_ROW_PADDING) but is a latent bug.

optimization_opportunities.description: Consolidate 11 nearly identical _sycl dispatch functions (dequantize_mul_mat_vec_q4_0_sycl through dequantize_mul_mat_vec_q6_K_sycl) into a single templated function. Each is 15-25 lines of identical boilerplate differing only in template parameters and quant constants. This is ~200 lines of pure duplication.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Maintenance cost reduction — changes need to be made in 1 place instead of 11. No runtime performance change.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Create a single template function parameterized on qk, qr, dequantize_kernel, sub_group_size, and ny. The switch in ggml_sycl_op_dequantize_mul_mat_vec can instantiate with appropriate parameters per quant type.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Pure refactor, no functional change.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace all dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor manual shuffle reductions with sycl::reduce_over_group(sub_group, tmp, sycl::plus<>()). All 8 kernel functions and both generic/reorder templates use the same manual dpct shuffle pattern. The sycl::reduce_over_group idiom is cleaner, compiles to optimal hardware-specific code, and is already used in mmvq reorder path.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-10% from better code generation on Intel. Significant code simplification.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace the reduction loop pattern (for mask = start; mask > 0; mask >>= 1) { tmp += dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor(...); } with tmp = sycl::reduce_over_group(item_ct1.get_sub_group(), tmp, sycl::plus<float>()); For the GGML_SYCL_F16 half2 path, reduce x and y components separately or use a custom operator.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Direct replacement. Need to handle the mask_start conditional (partial reduction when ncols <= GGML_SYCL_DMMV_X) — may need to zero out inactive lane values before full reduction.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add vectorized Y loads using sycl::vec<float,2> or float2 to match CUDA's y2 pointer pattern. Currently all Y data is loaded with scalar float loads. CUDA uses float2 (64-bit loads) for Y data throughout, doubling memory throughput for the Y vector. K-quant kernels could also benefit from 128-bit loads for weight blocks.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-20% memory throughput improvement for Y vector access
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Cast y pointer to sycl::vec<float,2>* and load pairs. For K-quant kernels, the strided access pattern (y[l+0], y[l+32]) makes this harder — would need to reorganize the inner loop to process contiguous pairs first.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Alignment requirements must be satisfied. K-quant kernels' strided Y access pattern may limit vectorization benefit.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add GLU/bias fusion support matching CUDA's has_fusion template parameter. CUDA fuses gate matmul + bias addition + GLU activation (swiglu, geglu, swiglu_oai) into the matvec kernel. SYCL dmmv has no fusion, requiring 3+ extra kernel launches and global memory round-trips for fused models.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 30-50% throughput improvement for models using GLU activations (most modern LLMs)
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add has_fusion template parameter. Add gate_x, x_bias, gate_bias pointer parameters. In the output write section, apply bias and GLU activation. Follow the pattern established in CUDA mmvf.cu lines 36-67 and 316-345.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires changes to the dispatch infrastructure to pass fusion arguments. May increase register pressure.

optimization_opportunities.description: Clean up DPCT migration artifacts: remove dpct::has_capability_or_fail() calls (6 instances on basic quant launchers), replace dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor with sycl native shuffle, convert item_ct1 naming to modern SYCL, convert 3D nd_range to 2D (dim 0 is always 1), remove __dpct_inline__ from dequantize functions.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Minor runtime improvement from removing dpct::has_capability_or_fail() overhead. Significant code readability improvement.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: has_capability_or_fail: remove entirely (capability checked at init). nd_range<3>: convert to nd_range<2> removing the unused first dimension. item_ct1: rename to item or nd_item. __dpct_inline__: replace with standard inline.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Cosmetic changes except for has_capability_or_fail removal which has a tiny runtime benefit.
